title: The week after the seller says yes
post:
The worst week to raise equity is the week after the seller says yes.

You have 60 to 90 days to close. The bank, the accountants, the lawyers and the seller all want your time. And you are on the phone with the fortieth family office, explaining the same deal again.

I did this as an independent sponsor. It is the part of the job nobody warns you about.

So at SourceCo we are moving the equity conversation earlier. Every deal on our marketplace can now get an Equity Pre-Check before you bid: a check of you and the deal, how much equity is likely, what has to be true, and a decision date for after you sign.

Sellers get a bid they can believe. You get your 90 days back. Link in the comments.

title: 312 dials
post:
312.

That is how many cold dials it takes our team to get one meeting with a business owner who is not for sale. We measured it across more than 22,000 calls.

Once an owner has engaged with us before, it drops to 39.

This is why good small companies rarely show up on a listing site. Finding them is slow, unglamorous work, and most buyers only ever see what a broker decided to market.

The full benchmark is free on our site. 20 industries, every number.

title: Four questions sellers ask
post:
Sellers and their bankers ask four questions about a sponsor's money:

1. How much equity is actually committed?
2. Who are the investors?
3. Do they get a say in big decisions?
4. What happens if one drops out?

Most support letters answer none of them.

That is why we built the Equity Pre-Check at SourceCo. On any deal from our marketplace, before you bid: a check of you and the deal, how much equity is likely, what still has to be true, and the date we will decide by once you sign. In writing, so you can show the seller.

It is not a promise to fund. It is an honest answer to the four questions, which is more than most bids come with. Link in the comments.

title: Why we built the Pre-Check
post:

What I needed back then was simple. Someone who had already looked at the deal and at me, who could say in writing how much equity they could likely bring, what had to be true, and when they would decide.

title: Problems found late kill more deals than money
post:
We talk a lot about equity as the reason sponsor deals die. The data says something else.

Axial looked at 75 small-company deals that fell apart after a signed offer in 2025. Problems found in the checks caused 25%. Quality of earnings gaps caused another 21%. Financing caused about 11%.

So almost half of broken deals died because of something in the business that nobody caught early enough. And when a sponsor's deal did fall apart, it had tied up the company for 129 days on average.

That is why our Equity Pre-Check looks at the deal, not just the money. Earnings quality, customer concentration, structure. Before you bid, not on day 60.

title: What founders remember
post:
A founder we worked with this year said something I keep thinking about:

"I'd previously been under LOI with a private equity firm and walked away when it became clear we were just a number."

He had a signed offer from a real fund and walked away anyway. 84 days after our first call, he closed with a different buyer.

Founders do not only pick the highest number. They pick the buyer they believe will close, and who will treat them like a person while they do it.

For sponsors, that is good news. You can win deals against funds. But only if the seller believes your money is real. Show them early.

title: A support letter is not a plan
post:
Most equity support letters say some version of "we are interested in reviewing this opportunity."

No amount. No conditions. No date.

Sellers know it. Fewer of them even ask for one now. In Axial's survey, the share of sponsors who are never asked for a support letter rose from about 27% to 39% in two years.

That does not mean sellers stopped caring about your money. It means the letters stopped telling them anything.

A useful one says four things: how much, what has to be true, who is behind it, and when they will decide. That is the format we use for the Equity Pre-Check.

Link in the comments.

title: Ask any equity partner
post:
Before you pick an equity partner for a deal, ask four questions:

1. How many deals have you actually funded, and what did each one raise?
2. Who makes the decision, and by when?
3. What does it cost me, all in?
4. What happens if one of your investors drops out after committing?

Good partners answer all four without flinching. We put our own answers on our page, including the hard one: Co-Invest is new, so our funded count today is zero. We will publish every raise as we go.

title: Never listed, 84 days

That is what off-market looks like. Not a secret list. A lot of calls and one good introduction.
